items.title: Concept: explicit transactions, then the event spine
items.body:
A mutation in Outline writes several rows: the change itself and an `events` row that websockets, webhooks, revisions and search all depend on. ADR-005 is about keeping those writes together; ADR-006 is about what happens to the event afterwards.

For ADR-005, read `server/middlewares/transaction.ts` (about 20 lines). Look up the difference between a *managed* and an *unmanaged* transaction in the Sequelize docs, then work out what the middleware's shape means for a route that succeeds and for one that fails. Read the rejected alternatives slowly: each names a failure mode, and the status line explains why the decision is weakening.

For ADR-006, open `server/models/Event.ts` and find the hook that hands a saved event to `globalEventQueue`. Note which hook it uses, what it does when a transaction is present, and the bug link in the comment. Then read the ADR's Negative consequences and ask: what happens to an event if the process stops at each point of that path?

The outbox capstone asks you to design a relay. While reading it, list every decision it makes: the marker column, old rows, step order, two relays at once, and the grace window. Write down why each choice is made.

excerpts.quote: Every mutation has a fan-out of side effects: websocket broadcasts to other

items.title: Why authorize() stops the handler with an error
items.body:
`authorize` calls `cannot()` and, when it is true, throws `AuthorizationError("Authorization error")`. Its return type is an assertion (`asserts target`), so nothing comes back on success. ADR-004 describes this as authorization being "an assertion, not a query": a handler cannot forget to check a returned value.

- *Returns false* describes `can()` or `cannot()`, not `authorize()`.
- *Returns a denial-reason string* is not in the code; `authorize` returns nothing.
- *Continues read-only* would need a downgrade path, and there is none: the throw ends the handler.

excerpts.quote: if (this.cannot(performer, action, target, options)) { throw AuthorizationError("Authorization error");

items.title: Why ADR-005 is marked Active-Eroding
items.body:
The Negative consequences give the reason directly: every command signature carries `transaction`, and forgetting to pass it compiles and passes low-concurrency tests. Enforcement is convention and review, not types, so nothing structural stops a new autocommit query from slipping in. That is what "Eroding" means here.

- *Back to ad hoc transactions*: that was the original starting point, rejected after partial commits; the ADR does not report a return to it.
- *Routes after the v1 API*: the ADR says the middleware wraps every mutating route and names no exception.
- *Dropped decorators*: typing ceremony is listed as a cost, but no one dropped the decorators.

excerpts.quote: this is why the status is Eroding: nothing structural stops a new autocommit

items.title: Why the event reaches the queue only after the commit
items.body:
`Event.enqueue` is an `@AfterSave` hook, but when the save had a transaction it does not enqueue right away. It registers `afterCommit` on `options.transaction.parent || options.transaction`, so the job is added once the outer transaction commits. The comment explains the `parent`: `findOrCreate` opens a child transaction whose own `afterCommit` would never fire. Without a transaction it enqueues at once.

- *Right away inside AfterSave*: that is only the no-transaction branch.
- *afterRollback*: no rollback hook exists; a rolled-back event is never published.
- *A cron sweep*: no relay exists today; building one is the capstone.

items.title: Why one failing action serializes as false
items.body:
`serialize()` first gathers the action names that apply to the performer and target, then checks each one inside its own `try`. The `catch` writes `output[action] = false` and the loop carries on, so the response still has a full policies object and the failing action is simply denied.

- *The error propagates*: the catch swallows it.
- *No entry*: the key is written, with the value false.
- *Set to true*: a failure never grants; failing closed is the point of the catch.

excerpts.quote: output[action] = this.can(performer, action, target); } catch (_err) { output[action] = false; }

items.title: Why getting into the queue is at-most-once
items.body:
ADR-006 separates two legs. From the queue onward, Bull retries jobs: at-least-once. But the event row commits first and the process publishes to Redis after, in-process. If the process crashes in between, the committed event never becomes a job, and no relay reconciles it. So the hand-off INTO the queue happens once or not at all.

- *Exactly-once*: the row and the Redis job are in different systems and cannot share a commit.
- *Bull retries the publish*: Bull retries jobs it already holds; a publish that never happened is not a job.
- *A relay re-sends*: the ADR says there is no relay; that is what the capstone builds.

excerpts.quote: at-least-once from the queue, but *at-most-once into* it. No relay reconciles the gap.

items.title: Why both writes roll back when the command throws
items.body:
The middleware is `sequelize.transaction(async (t) => { ctx.state.transaction = t; return next(); })`. That is a managed transaction: Sequelize commits when the callback's promise resolves and rolls back when it rejects. `next()` runs the whole rest of the route inside the callback, so a throw after two writes that used `ctx.state.transaction` rejects the callback and undoes both.

- *Each query autocommits*: only a query that is NOT given the transaction autocommits; these two were given it.
- *Only the second rolls back*: the two writes share one transaction, so they succeed or fail together.
- *Both commit*: the commit happens only on a resolved callback.

excerpts.quote: await sequelize.transaction(async (t: Transaction) => { ctx.state.transaction = t; return next(); });

items.title: Concept: one policy engine for the API and the UI
items.body:
Outline's permissions depend on the object: team, collection, membership, sharing and archive state all combine. ADR-004 puts every rule in one in-house engine, `server/policies/cancan.ts`, plus one policy file per model (`server/policies/document.ts`, `collection.ts`, ...). The same rules also travel to the browser, so the UI can hide a button the server would refuse.

Read `cancan.ts` top to bottom; it is under 300 lines. Answer these from the code:

- What does `allow()` store, and how is the index keyed?
- Which abilities does `getMatchingAbilities` collect for a given performer, action and target? Note the special action name it also looks up.
- In `can()`, which kinds of value may a condition return, and how are the results combined into the return value? Compare what you find with the ADR's Negative consequences.
- What do `cannot()` and `authorize()` add on top of `can()`?
- How does `serialize()` decide which actions to include, and how does it treat each one?

Then open `app/models/Policy.ts` to see the client side of the same object.

excerpts.quote: The same rules must gate API requests **and** drive UI affordances

readMore.why: The whole engine: allow, can, cannot, authorize and serialize.
The most complex composed policy, built from the engine above.

items.title: Why a string condition result comes back as a membership array
items.body:
In `can()`, every truthy result that is a string is pushed to `membershipIds`; a `true` result only sets `hasNonMembershipMatch`. The function then returns `membershipIds` when it is non-empty, otherwise the boolean. So a single condition returning `"m1"` makes `can()` return `["m1"]`, which is truthy and grants the ability.

- *false, as a denial reason*: ADR-004 line 54 says "string = denial reason", but the code treats the string as a grant that carries membership ids. The code is keyed; the ADR wording is wrong here.
- *true*: the boolean is returned only when no string result was seen.
- *The string itself*: strings are collected into an array, not returned one by one.

excerpts.quote: Conditions may return `boolean | string` (string = denial reason)

items.title: Start here: four ADRs and one capstone in a real Outline checkout
items.body:
This quest studies Outline, a real collaborative wiki, through the teaching docs added next to its code. `fabledocs3/` holds ten architecture decision records (ADRs); each one states a context, the decision, the rejected alternatives, the consequences, and an **Evidence** list of files. `fabledocs4/` turns the weak spots those ADRs admit into drills and capstones.

Read in this order:

1. `fabledocs3/adr-004-policy-authorization.md` (who may do what).
2. `fabledocs3/adr-005-sequelize-explicit-transactions.md` (how a mutation stays atomic).
3. `fabledocs3/adr-006-event-spine.md` (how side effects leave the request).
4. `fabledocs3/adr-007-crdt-triple-representation.md` (real-time editing and its storage).
5. `fabledocs4/02-capstone-outbox-relay.md` (a design exercise built on ADR-006).

For every ADR, open each file in its Evidence list before you move on. The quiz asks what the CODE does, and an ADR is a summary written by a person: when the two disagree, trust the code. Keep a note of each place where you find such a difference.

excerpts.quote: Authorization here is per-object and conditional, not role-lookup

readMore.why: The index of all ten ADRs and how they depend on each other.
How the drills, capstones and labs in fabledocs4 fit together.

items.title: Why FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED keeps two relays apart
items.body:
`FOR UPDATE` locks the rows a relay selects until its transaction ends. `SKIP LOCKED` makes a second relay's SELECT pass over rows that are already locked instead of waiting for them, so each pod claims a different batch and no event is enqueued twice by two pods.

- *ORDER BY ... LIMIT 100*: picks a batch but takes no lock, so both pods can select the same 100 rows.
- *FOR SHARE*: a shared lock lets both pods hold the same rows at once.
- *SET LOCAL lock_timeout*: limits how long a lock wait may last; it does not keep two readers apart.

readMore.why: The SQL lab where the capstone expects you to practise SKIP LOCKED.

items.title: Why a document with state loads without a lock
items.body:
`onLoadDocument` first reads only the `state` attribute with `Document.unscoped().findOne`, outside any transaction. If state exists it applies it to a new `Y.Doc` and returns. The locked path, a transaction with `lock: transaction.LOCK.UPDATE` plus a second check of state, runs only for a legacy document with no state yet, which is then built from `content` or `text`.

- *Locks FOR UPDATE and rebuilds from content*: that is the legacy-document path.
- *Rebuilds from markdown text*: text is the last fallback for a document with neither state nor content.
- *A 15s lock_timeout*: that `SET LOCAL` lives in `documentCollaborativeUpdater`, the write-back path.

excerpts.quote: If the document already has state, we can return it without needing a transaction

items.title: Why implicit CLS propagation was rejected
items.body:
ADR-005 lists AsyncLocalStorage/CLS as alternative 3 and rejects it for its failure mode: when async context is lost (a stray timer, a callback boundary), the query runs outside the transaction and autocommits, and nothing reports it. Passing the transaction as a parameter fails visibly in review instead.

- *Conflicts with Koa*: the ADR names no compile problem, and CLS is a runtime mechanism.
- *Doubled latency*: no measurement is mentioned anywhere in the ADR.
- *Support dropped*: the ADR says Sequelize supports it; the objection is about how it fails.

items.title: Why the relay publishes before it marks
items.body:
With publish-then-mark, a crash after the enqueue but before the UPDATE leaves the row unpublished, so the next sweep enqueues it again: a duplicate. Duplicates are survivable when consumers are idempotent. With mark-then-publish, a crash or a failed enqueue after the UPDATE leaves the row marked as sent although no job exists, and nothing will ever retry it: the loss the relay was built to remove.

- *Holding the lock across Redis*: both orders run in the same claiming transaction; the order of the two steps does not change the lock.
- *publishedAt in the payload*: the job carries the event, not the marker.
- *Fast path skips the row*: the fast path never reads `publishedAt`; the relay sweeps only rows older than the grace window.

items.title: Why old rows need publishedAt = createdAt
items.body:
The relay claims rows `WHERE "publishedAt" IS NULL`. If the migration left every existing row NULL, the first relay run would treat years of already-published events as unpublished and enqueue them all again: a replay storm. Backfilling `publishedAt = createdAt` marks history as already sent.

- *A partial index needs no NULLs*: the capstone asks for a partial index WHERE NULL, which is exactly the rows it targets.
- *Postgres refuses a nullable column*: adding a nullable column is allowed on a table with rows.
- *CleanupOldEventsTask deletes NULL rows*: that task selects by `createdAt` against a 365-day cutoff; it never reads `publishedAt`.

excerpts.quote: and why must it not be NULL for them? (If old rows look unpublished, your relay replays history
